## Elementary row operations and matrices

::: {#prp-smh:elemradop}
Suppose $B$ is obtained by applying an elementary row operation to the $m\times n$-matrix $A$. 
Then $B=EA$ where $E$ is the matrix obtained by applying the same row operation to the identity matrix $I_m$.
:::

A matrix is called *elementary* if it is obtained by applying an elementary row operation to the identity matrix: 
$$
\begin{aligned}
E_1 &=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} & \text{ corresponds to } I+2II \\
E_2 &=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{pmatrix} & \text{ corresponds to } 3III \\
E_3 &=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} & \text{ corresponds to } I \leftrightarrow II
\end{aligned}
$$

---

## Reversing elementary row operations

Row operations can be reversed: 

\begin{align*}
F_1 &=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} & \text{ corresponds to } I-2II \\
F_2 &=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1/3 \end{pmatrix} & \text{ corresponds to } III/3 \\
F_3 &=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} & \text{ corresponds to } I \leftrightarrow II
\end{align*}

---

$F_i$ reverses $E_i$, meaning that $F_1E_1=I_n$, $F_2E_2=I_n$, $F_3E_3=I_n$, 
which is easily verified: 

```{python}
#| echo: true
import numpy as np

E_1 = np.array([[1,2,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]])
F_1 = np.array([[1,-2,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]])
E_1 @ F_1
```

---

::: {#prp-}
For every matrix $A$ we can write 
$$C=E_k\cdots E_2E_1A$$
where $C$ is a matrix on reduced echelon form, and where $E_1,E_2,...,E_k$ are elementary matrices.
:::

::: {#prp-}
Assume a system is obtained from another by applying an elementary row operation. 
Then the two systems have the same solutions. 
:::
